title: IRS, Limited Liability Company (LLC), federal tax classification
text:
## LLC federal tax classification (general information, not legal or tax advice)

This is general educational information. Entity and tax rules vary by state and change over time; confirm specifics with a licensed attorney and a qualified tax advisor before relying on them.

The IRS states that a Limited Liability Company (LLC) is a business structure allowed by state statute. Owners of an LLC are called members. Most states do not restrict ownership, so members may be individuals, corporations, other LLCs, and foreign entities, and there is no maximum number of members in most states.

## Default classification depends on member count

For federal income tax purposes, an LLC is not a distinct entity type on the tax return; instead it is classified by default rules. A domestic LLC with at least two members is classified as a partnership for federal income tax purposes unless it files Form 8832 and affirmatively elects to be treated as a corporation. An LLC with only one member is treated as an entity disregarded as separate from its owner (a disregarded entity), unless it files Form 8832 and elects corporate treatment.

## Check-the-box election (Form 8832)

An LLC can change its default classification using Form 8832, Entity Classification Election. An election cannot take effect more than 75 days prior to the date the election is filed, nor can it take effect later than 12 months after the date the election is filed.

## Key nuance: disregarded is not disregarded for all taxes

Even though a single-member LLC is disregarded for income tax, it is treated as a separate entity for employment tax and certain excise taxes. This is a common point of confusion for founders. Because default LLC treatment is pass-through, income and losses generally flow to members' personal returns, which is one reason venture-backed startups typically prefer a C-corporation instead (a C-corp is a taxable entity that can more cleanly issue preferred stock and stock options to investors and employees).

title: Delaware Division of Corporations, About the Agency (why Delaware)
text:
## Why startups incorporate in Delaware (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about a common jurisdiction choice; confirm the right choice for a specific company with a licensed attorney.

The Delaware Division of Corporations reports that Delaware is home to more than 2 million business entities, and that more than 66% of the Fortune 500 have chosen Delaware as their legal home. This concentration is a large part of why venture investors and startup lawyers default to a Delaware C-corporation: investors and their counsel are already familiar with Delaware corporate law and its documents.

## The Delaware General Corporation Law (DGCL)

Delaware describes its General Corporation Law as the most advanced and flexible business formation statute in the nation. Familiar, flexible statutory rules reduce friction and legal cost in financings and governance.

## The Court of Chancery

Delaware has a specialized business court, the Court of Chancery, established more than 225 years ago, that has written most of the modern U.S. corporation case law. Because disputes are decided by expert judges (not juries) applying a deep, predictable body of precedent, outcomes are more predictable, which lowers legal risk for companies and investors. The combination of a sophisticated statute, an expert equity court, and a large body of case law is the practical reason a Delaware C-corporation is the conventional structure for a venture-backed startup.

title: IRS, S Corporations (election, eligibility, pass-through)
text:
## S corporation basics (general information, not legal or tax advice)

This is general educational information; tax rules change and vary by situation, so confirm with a qualified tax advisor and a licensed attorney.

The IRS defines S corporations as corporations that elect to pass corporate income, losses, deductions, and credits through to their shareholders for federal tax purposes. Shareholders report the flow-through of income and losses on their personal tax returns and are assessed tax at their individual income tax rates. This allows S corporations to avoid double taxation on the corporate income (unlike a C-corporation, where the corporation pays tax and shareholders pay again on dividends).

## Eligibility requirements to elect S status

To qualify for S corporation status, the corporation must: be a domestic corporation; have only allowable shareholders (individuals, certain trusts, and estates, and may not be partnerships, corporations, or non-resident alien shareholders); have no more than 100 shareholders; have only one class of stock; and not be an ineligible corporation (certain financial institutions, insurance companies, and domestic international sales corporations).

## Election form and startup relevance

To elect S status, the corporation files Form 2553, Election by a Small Business Corporation, signed by all shareholders. The one-class-of-stock rule and the ban on entity or non-resident-alien shareholders are exactly why venture-backed startups usually do NOT elect S status: they plan to issue preferred stock to venture funds (often partnerships or foreign investors), which an S corporation cannot do. This is a classic reason the C-corporation is chosen for a fundraising startup even though it carries potential double taxation.

title: Y Combinator, SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) document set
text:
## The SAFE, what it is (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about a widely used template; the right instrument and terms for a specific raise should be confirmed with a licensed attorney.

A SAFE is a simple agreement for future equity, introduced by Y Combinator in late 2013. It is an early-stage fundraising instrument that converts into equity during a later priced round (typically the Series A). It lets founders and investors set the terms of an investment with minimal negotiation and legal overhead, and it is NOT debt: unlike a convertible note, a standard SAFE has no interest rate and no maturity date, so it does not create a repayment obligation or a ticking deadline.

## High-resolution fundraising and efficiency

The SAFE enables high-resolution fundraising: a startup can close with each investor individually as that investor is ready, rather than coordinating a single simultaneous close. As a single-document security with only a few negotiable terms, it reduces legal fees and negotiation time.

## The post-money SAFE variants (US)

Y Combinator replaced the original pre-money SAFE with the post-money SAFE in 2018. For US companies it offers three primary versions: Safe: Valuation Cap, no Discount; Safe: Discount, no Valuation Cap; and Safe: 'Uncapped MFN' (no Valuation Cap, no Discount). An optional Pro Rata Side Letter accompanies these. International variants exist for Canada, the Caymans, and Singapore. The key change in the post-money SAFE is that the valuation cap is measured after (post) all SAFE money is counted, which makes the investor's ownership percentage easier to calculate but means founder dilution from stacked SAFEs is higher than many founders expect.

## Conversion and the SAFE User Guide

The post-money SAFE converts when a priced financing occurs. Y Combinator publishes a SAFE User Guide with sample calculations and conversion explanations. A common founder mistake is issuing many uncapped or high-cap SAFEs without modeling the combined conversion, then being surprised at the Series A by how much of the company the SAFEs claim once they all convert at once.

title: National Venture Capital Association (NVCA), Model Legal Documents
text:
## The NVCA model legal documents (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about widely used industry templates; the terms of any actual financing should be negotiated and confirmed with a licensed attorney.

The National Venture Capital Association (NVCA) publishes a suite of model legal documents that have become the industry standard for a priced preferred-stock venture financing (for example a Series A). Because both sides' counsel start from the same familiar forms, the documents reduce transaction costs and time and establish industry norms. A startup lawyer should know what each document does.

## The core financing set

The Term Sheet is the short, mostly non-binding summary of the deal economics and control terms that precedes the long-form documents. The Stock Purchase Agreement governs the terms and conditions under which investors purchase the preferred equity, including representations and warranties. The Certificate of Incorporation (amended and restated) sets the corporate charter, the authorized shares, and the rights, preferences, and privileges of the preferred stock (liquidation preference, dividends, conversion, anti-dilution, protective provisions). The Investors' Rights Agreement defines investor rights such as information rights, registration rights, and pro rata (preemptive) rights. The Voting Agreement establishes board composition and drag-along arrangements among shareholders. The Right of First Refusal and Co-Sale Agreement regulates transfer restrictions, letting the company and investors participate in or block founder stock sales and protecting against unwanted transfers.

## Supporting documents

The Management Rights Letter gives a venture fund the consultation rights it often needs for its own regulatory (VCOC) status. The Model Indemnification Agreement provides liability protection for directors and officers. A Model Legal Opinion offers template opinion language. The set also includes confidential disclosure agreements and shareholder questionnaires. Knowing this document map lets counsel spot when a term sheet quietly deviates from market norms.

title: SEC / Investor.gov, Accredited Investors (Updated Investor Bulletin)
text:
## Who is an accredited investor (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about U.S. securities rules; a specific offering's compliance should be confirmed with a licensed securities attorney.

When a startup raises money by selling stock or SAFEs, it is selling securities, which by default must be registered with the SEC unless an exemption applies. Most startup rounds rely on the private-placement exemption (Regulation D), which generally requires that investors be accredited investors. The SEC investor bulletin explains that the definition exists to ensure that participating investors are financially sophisticated and able to fend for themselves or sustain the risk of loss.

## The financial tests

An individual qualifies through earned income exceeding $200,000 (or $300,000 together with a spouse or spousal equivalent) in each of the prior two years, with a reasonable expectation of the same for the current year. Alternatively, an individual qualifies with a net worth over $1 million, either alone or together with a spouse or spousal equivalent, excluding the value of the person's primary residence.

## Professional and entity criteria

A person may also qualify by holding in good standing a Series 7 (General Securities Representative), Series 65 (Investment Adviser Representative), or Series 82 (Private Securities Offerings Representative) license. Entities can qualify if they have total assets exceeding $5 million (and were not formed specifically to acquire the securities), total investments exceeding $5 million, or if all of the entity's equity owners are themselves accredited investors. A frequent founder mistake is taking money from friends and family who are not accredited without a compliant exemption, which can create rescission rights and jeopardize future financings.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, 26 U.S. Code Section 83 (property transferred for services; 83(b) election)
text:
## Section 83 and the 83(b) election (general information, not legal or tax advice)

This is a general educational summary of a tax statute; the 83(b) decision is fact-specific and time-critical, so confirm with a qualified tax advisor and a licensed attorney before acting.

26 U.S. Code Section 83 governs property (such as founder restricted stock or early-exercised options) transferred in connection with the performance of services. The general rule (subsection (a)) is that the excess of the fair market value of the property, determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse, over the amount (if any) paid for the property, is included in the service provider's gross income at the first time the rights are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever occurs earlier. In plain terms, without an election you are taxed as the stock vests, on the value at each vesting date.

## Substantial risk of forfeiture

Under subsection (c)(1), rights are subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture when the person's rights to full enjoyment of the property are conditioned upon the future performance of substantial services. Standard four-year vesting is exactly such a condition, which is why unvested founder stock is normally taxed only as it vests unless the holder elects otherwise.

## The subsection (b) election and the 30-day rule

Subsection (b) lets the service provider elect to include the spread in gross income in the year of transfer instead. The statute requires that the election be made in the manner the Secretary prescribes and be made not later than 30 days after the date of such transfer. Filing an 83(b) election within 30 days lets a founder pay tax now on a typically tiny value at grant (often near zero), starting the capital gains holding period, rather than paying ordinary income tax on potentially large value as the shares vest. The classic, unfixable mistake is missing the 30-day deadline: it is strict, and if elected the property is later forfeited, no deduction is allowed for the forfeiture. The IRS also released Form 15620 as a standardized way to make the election, though a compliant written statement is still permitted.

title: USPTO, Patent essentials (types, term, requirements)
text:
## Patent essentials (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information; patent strategy is complex and jurisdiction-specific, so confirm with a registered patent attorney or agent.

A U.S. patent grants an inventor the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention. Importantly, this is the right to stop others, not necessarily the right to make the invention yourself, and patents are effective only within U.S. territory (protection in other countries requires filing there).

## Three types of patents

Utility patents cover new or improved processes, machines, articles of manufacture, or compositions of matter. Design patents protect new, original, ornamental designs for manufactured articles. Plant patents cover distinct, new plant varieties that are asexually reproduced.

## Patent terms

Utility and plant patents last up to 20 years from the earliest filing date. Design patents last 15 years from the grant date. Utility patent holders must pay maintenance fees on schedule to keep the patent in force.

## Requirements for patentability

To be patentable, an invention must be useful (functional, not merely theoretical), be described clearly enough to teach how to make and use it, be novel (new, not previously done), and be non-obvious relative to existing inventions. The United States uses a first-inventor-to-file system, so timing of the filing matters. A common startup mistake is publicly disclosing, selling, or demoing an invention before filing at least a provisional application, which can start clocks and bars that destroy patentability, so counsel typically advises filing before any public disclosure.

title: USPTO, Strong trademarks (the spectrum of distinctiveness)
text:
## Choosing a strong trademark (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information; clearing and registering a mark should be confirmed with a licensed trademark attorney.

Not all trademarks are equally protectable. The USPTO describes a spectrum of distinctiveness that determines how strong and registrable a mark is. A top-1% counsel steers founders toward the strong end early, before the brand and domain are locked in.

## Strong marks

Fanciful marks are invented words with meaning only in relation to the goods or services, such as Exxon for petroleum or Pepsi for soft drinks. Arbitrary marks use real words unrelated to the goods, such as Apple for computers. Suggestive marks imply a quality without directly describing it, such as Coppertone for sun-tanning products. These are the strongest and let you most easily prevent others from using the mark.

## Weak or unregistrable marks

Descriptive marks merely describe a feature of the goods or services, such as Creamy for yogurt; they cannot be registered on the Principal Register unless they acquire distinctiveness (secondary meaning) through extensive use in commerce over many years. Generic marks are the common name for the goods or services, such as Bicycle for bicycles or Bagel Shop for a bagel shop; they do not indicate source and can never function as trademarks. Weak marks can be difficult and costly to defend and often remain federally unregistrable. The classic mistake is falling in love with a descriptive or generic name because it explains the product, then being unable to protect it or being blocked by an earlier user.

title: USPTO, Trade secret policy (definition, elements, DTSA)
text:
## Trade secrets (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information; a trade secret protection program should be confirmed with a licensed attorney.

The USPTO defines a trade secret as information that has actual or potential independent economic value by virtue of not being generally known, that derives value from not being readily ascertainable by others who could obtain economic value from its disclosure or use, and that is subject to reasonable efforts to maintain its secrecy. All three elements are required; if any one is lost, trade secret status ceases. Unlike patents, trade secrets have no fixed duration and can last indefinitely as long as the conditions are maintained (the Coca-Cola formula is the classic example).

## Key legislation

Most U.S. states have adopted a version of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (UTSA). At the federal level, the Economic Espionage Act of 1996 established federal criminal trade secret protections, and the Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 (DTSA) created a federal civil cause of action for trade secret misappropriation.

## Trade secrets versus patents

Patents require public disclosure of the invention and offer a limited term (generally 20 years for utility patents), while trade secrets require secrecy and can last indefinitely but offer no protection against independent discovery or reverse engineering. A frequent startup mistake is relying on trade secret protection while taking no reasonable measures to keep the information secret, for example not using confidentiality agreements, not restricting access, and not marking documents confidential; without reasonable measures, the legal protection evaporates.

title: Common Paper, Mutual NDA Standard Terms (CC BY 4.0)
text:
## The mutual NDA (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about a free, openly licensed (CC BY 4.0) standard template; adapt and confirm any actual agreement with a licensed attorney.

A mutual non-disclosure agreement (MNDA) lets two parties share confidential information while evaluating whether to enter into a business relationship. The Common Paper MNDA separates a short Cover Page (the deal-specific choices) from the versioned Standard Terms hosted online, so any modifications appear only on the Cover Page and the referenced Standard Terms (for example Version 1.0) remain permanently unchanged. This structure keeps the legal text stable and readable.

## Definition of Confidential Information and standard exclusions

Information is Confidential Information when it is either explicitly identified as such or should be reasonably understood as confidential or proprietary due to its nature and the circumstances of disclosure (technical details, designs, pricing, security documentation, roadmaps). The receiving party has no obligation for information that is or becomes publicly available through no fault of the receiving party, was rightfully in its possession before disclosure, was rightfully received from a third party without restriction, or was independently developed without reference to the shared information. These four carve-outs are standard and their absence is a red flag in a one-sided NDA.

## Obligations and term

The receiving party must use the information only for the stated Purpose, limit disclosure (except to employees and advisors with a need to know who are bound to confidentiality), and protect it using at least the same care it uses for its own similar information but no less than a reasonable standard of care. The agreement distinguishes the MNDA Term (the window when sharing occurs) from the Term of Confidentiality (how long protection lasts); Common Paper notes many NDAs use a one-year sharing period with a two-year protection period, and that most use a fixed term rather than perpetual confidentiality. A common mistake is signing a broad, perpetual, one-way NDA without these standard exclusions, which can inadvertently restrict the company's own later work.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, At-will employment
text:
## At-will employment (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information; employment law varies by state and by facts, so confirm specifics with a licensed employment attorney.

Cornell LII defines at-will employment as an arrangement in which the employee may quit at any time, and the employer may fire the employee for any reason and at any point, so long as the dismissal is not for an unlawful reason. The doctrine is the default in 49 U.S. states when there is no express or implied employment agreement. Montana is the sole exception: it requires good cause for dismissals after the probationary period.

## Unlawful-reason limits

At-will does not mean an employer can fire for any reason whatsoever. Employers cannot terminate at-will employees for discriminatory reasons such as their race, religion, or sex, cannot retaliate against an employee for reporting harassment, and cannot fire an employee because the employee exercised a legal right. So the practical rule is at-will termination is permitted unless a specific statute or public policy makes the particular reason unlawful.

## Startup relevance

Most U.S. startup offer letters state that employment is at-will, and counsel typically keeps that language consistent across the offer letter, handbook, and any equity documents. A common mistake is undercutting at-will status by making oral promises of continued employment or writing handbooks that imply for-cause-only termination, which courts can treat as an implied contract that overrides at-will.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Independent contractor (classification)
text:
## Employee vs independent contractor (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information; worker classification is fact-specific and tested differently under tax law, wage-and-hour law, and state law, so confirm with a licensed attorney before classifying anyone.

Cornell LII describes independent contractors as entities hired by employers to accomplish certain tasks but over whom the employer does not have the right of control. The central question is control: independent contractors control the manner and means of their own work, tend to have specialized skills or knowledge, and work for many clients, distinguishing them from employees who work under employer direction. Courts and agencies also look at the economic realities of the relationship, not just a label in a contract.

## Why misclassification matters

The stakes are financial and legal. Independent contractors must pay their own Social Security and Medicare taxes, while employers generally pay a share for employees, so misclassifying an employee as a contractor can create back-tax and penalty exposure. Under tort law, employers who hire genuine independent contractors usually have no vicarious liability for the contractor's tortious acts (with exceptions for non-delegable duties such as inherently dangerous activities), but they can be liable for their own negligence in selecting a contractor. Wage-and-hour, benefits, and unemployment rules also turn on the classification.

## The classic startup mistake

A very common and costly startup mistake is treating early team members as 1099 independent contractors when the company actually controls their schedule, tools, and manner of work, especially engineers building the core product. If they are really employees, the company can face reclassification, back employment taxes, penalties, wage claims, and, critically for IP, weaker IP ownership if a proper written assignment was not signed (work made for hire and default IP rules treat contractors differently from employees). Calling someone a contractor does not make them one; the facts control.

title: GDPR, Article 5 (Principles relating to processing of personal data)
GDPR, Article 6 (Lawfulness of processing, the six lawful bases)
California Privacy Protection Agency, CCPA/CPRA consumer rights and thresholds
text:
## California Consumer Privacy Act (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about California law; the specific compliance obligations for a business should be confirmed with a licensed privacy attorney.

The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (CCPA) established privacy protections for California consumers. In 2020, voters approved Proposition 24, the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA), which amended and expanded the CCPA; the CPRA amendments took effect January 1, 2023, and created the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) to implement and enforce the law. The CPPA promotes awareness, adopts regulations, and enforces compliance through investigations and audits.

## Consumer rights

California residents have the right to know what personal information a business collects, the sources, the purposes, and the third parties it is shared with; the right to delete personal information (with exceptions); the right to correct inaccurate personal information; the right to opt out of the sale or sharing (for cross-context behavioral advertising) of their personal information; the right to limit the use of sensitive personal information to limited purposes such as providing the requested services; and the right to non-discrimination for exercising these rights.

## Who must comply (thresholds)

The CCPA applies to for-profit businesses doing business in California that meet at least one threshold: annual gross revenue over $26.625 million (as adjusted, effective January 1, 2025); or buy, sell, or share the personal information of 100,000 or more California residents or households; or derive 50 percent or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing residents' personal information. A common startup mistake is assuming CCPA does not apply because the company is small or not based in California; the thresholds turn on doing business in California and the volume or revenue tests, not on the company's home state, so an out-of-state SaaS startup can be covered.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Piercing the corporate veil
text:
## Piercing the corporate veil (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information; whether liability protection holds in a given situation is fact-specific, so confirm with a licensed attorney.

Forming a corporation or LLC normally gives the owners limited liability: creditors of the business generally cannot reach the personal assets of shareholders. Cornell LII notes courts presume against piercing the corporate veil because limited liability encourages the development of public markets for stock and the liquidity and diversification benefits investors receive. But courts will put aside limited liability and hold a corporation's shareholders or directors personally liable for the corporation's actions or debts when there is serious misconduct and fairly egregious actions.

## The factors courts weigh

Common factors that justify veil piercing include the alter ego or instrumentality doctrine (the corporation operates as a mere extension of the shareholder), commingling of assets (intermingling of personal and corporate funds), undercapitalization (insufficient capital at incorporation), failure to observe corporate formalities (not keeping the business separate through minutes, resolutions, and separate accounts), and fraud (creating or using the entity to escape liability). Under the alter ego doctrine, a shareholder who uses the corporation as his agent to conduct business in an individual capacity can be held vicariously liable.

## The practical lesson for founders

The single most preventable trigger is commingling personal and company funds. Founders protect their limited liability by keeping a separate company bank account, not paying personal expenses from company funds, signing contracts in the company's name, adequately capitalizing the company, and observing basic corporate formalities (board consents, annual filings). Treating the company checking account like a personal wallet is the classic mistake that lets a plaintiff argue the corporation is a sham and reach the founder's personal assets.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Business judgment rule (director duties)
text:
## Director duties and the business judgment rule (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about corporate governance; how these duties apply to a specific board decision should be confirmed with a licensed attorney.

Directors of a corporation owe fiduciary duties, principally the duty of care and the duty of loyalty, to the corporation and its shareholders. The business judgment rule is the doctrine that protects directors from liability for honest, informed decisions. Cornell LII explains that courts uphold director decisions, giving directors immunity from liability for duty-of-care claims, when the decision is made (1) in good faith, (2) with the care that a reasonably prudent person would use, and (3) with the reasonable belief that the director is acting in the best interests of the corporation.

## A presumption, and how it is rebutted

The rule operates as a presumption in favor of the board, so courts generally refrain from second-guessing good-faith business decisions, and the burden of proof shifts to the plaintiff. The presumption is defeated if the plaintiff proves gross negligence or bad faith or a conflict of interest (self-dealing). If the rule does not apply, the board must demonstrate that both the process and the substance of the transaction were fair (the entire fairness standard).

## Startup relevance

For a startup board, the practical lesson is process: directors who inform themselves, avoid undisclosed conflicts, and act in good faith are broadly protected, while those who rubber-stamp a related-party deal or ignore obvious red flags lose that protection. The duty of loyalty is where founders most often stumble, for example approving a transaction in which a director or their fund has a personal financial interest without proper disclosure and disinterested approval.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, 17 U.S. Code Section 106 (exclusive rights in copyrighted works)
text:
## The exclusive rights of copyright (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information reproducing statutory text; how copyright applies to a specific work or license should be confirmed with a licensed attorney.

17 U.S. Code Section 106 gives the owner of a copyright the exclusive rights to do and to authorize the following: (1) to reproduce the copyrighted work in copies or phonorecords; (2) to prepare derivative works based upon the copyrighted work; (3) to distribute copies or phonorecords of the copyrighted work to the public by sale or other transfer of ownership, or by rental, lease, or lending; (4) in the case of literary, musical, dramatic, and choreographic works, pantomimes, and motion pictures and other audiovisual works, to perform the copyrighted work publicly; (5) in the case of literary, musical, dramatic, and choreographic works, pantomimes, and pictorial, graphic, or sculptural works, including the individual images of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, to display the copyrighted work publicly; and (6) in the case of sound recordings, to perform the copyrighted work publicly by means of a digital audio transmission. These rights are subject to the limitations in sections 107 through 122 (for example fair use in section 107).

## Why this matters to a startup

Copyright arises automatically when an original work (including source code, designs, copy, and documentation) is fixed in a tangible medium. Because these exclusive rights initially belong to the author or creator, the key startup issue is chain of title: the company only owns the code and content if the people who created it (founders, employees, and especially contractors) assigned their copyright to the company in writing. Relying on someone else's copyrighted template, image, or code without a license is copyright infringement, and using an open-source component without complying with its license (for example a copyleft license) can create obligations the company did not intend.

title: SEC / Investor.gov, Private Placements under Regulation D (Rule 506(b) and 506(c))
text:
## Raising money privately under Regulation D (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about U.S. securities exemptions; any actual offering should be structured and confirmed with a licensed securities attorney.

Most startup equity rounds are private placements: offerings exempt from the SEC's registration requirements pursuant to Securities Act Section 4(a)(2) or its safe harbor under Regulation D. Selling stock or SAFEs is selling securities, so the company must fit an exemption or register.

## Rule 506(b) versus Rule 506(c)

Under Rule 506(b), the issuer may not use general solicitation or advertising, may sell to an unlimited number of accredited investors but to no more than 35 non-accredited investors, and those non-accredited investors must be financially sophisticated; if any non-accredited investors participate, the issuer must provide specified disclosures. Under Rule 506(c), the issuer may use general solicitation and advertising, but only accredited investors are allowed to purchase, and the issuer must take reasonable steps to verify each purchaser's accredited investor status (a self-checked box is not enough).

## Form D and restricted securities

Issuers must file a Form D with the SEC no later than 15 days after they first sell securities in the offering. Most private-placement securities are restricted, meaning an investor should be prepared to hold the securities indefinitely, and resale generally requires a holding period of six months to one year depending on whether the company is a reporting company. A common startup mistake is publicly advertising a raise (for example tweeting we are raising, come invest) while intending to rely on Rule 506(b), which forbids general solicitation, potentially blowing the exemption.

title: U.S. Copyright Office, Copyright in General (FAQ)
text:
## Copyright basics (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information from the U.S. Copyright Office; how copyright applies to specific works or disputes should be confirmed with a licensed attorney.

Copyright is a form of intellectual property law that protects original works of authorship including literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works, such as poetry, novels, movies, songs, computer software, and architecture. Copyright does not protect facts, ideas, systems, or methods of operation, although it may protect the way these things are expressed. This idea/expression distinction is why a startup cannot copyright a business idea itself, only the specific expression (the actual code, copy, and designs).

## Protection is automatic; registration adds rights

A work is under copyright protection the moment it is created and fixed in a tangible form that is perceptible either directly or with the aid of a machine or device. Registration is voluntary, but you will have to register if you wish to bring a lawsuit for infringement of a U.S. work. Timely registration provides significant advantages, including the ability to seek statutory damages and attorney's fees in successful litigation, and a registration made before or within five years of publication serves as prima facie evidence of the validity of the copyright.

## Copyright versus patent and trademark

Copyright safeguards creative works like books and songs; a utility patent protects new inventions or processes; and a trademark protects words, phrases, symbols, or designs that identify the source of goods or services. Founders frequently confuse these; the practical rule is that code and content are copyright, brand names and logos are trademark, and inventions are patent, and a company needs the right protection (and the right written assignments) for each.

title: Bonterms, Standard commercial agreements (community-drafted, CC BY 4.0)
text:
## Standardized commercial contracts (general information, not legal advice)

This is general educational information about free, openly licensed templates; adapt any actual agreement to the deal and confirm with a licensed attorney.

Bonterms provides free-to-use, neutral commercial agreements developed by a standing committee of more than 120 lawyers, vetted for best practices, usability, and alignment with prevailing market norms. Like Common Paper, Bonterms separates a deal-specific Cover Page from versioned Standard Terms, and the documents are released under CC BY 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution), so a startup can adopt them freely with attribution and even display a We Use Bonterms logo.

## The document set a startup lawyer should know

The published standard agreements include the Mutual NDA and One-Way NDA (confidentiality), Cloud Terms and Online Cloud Terms (the master SaaS subscription agreement that governs how customers use the product), the Software License Terms and End User Agreement, the Professional Services Agreement (for implementation or consulting work, the analog of an MSA plus SOW), the Service Level Agreement (uptime and support commitments), the AI Addendum, the Data Protection Addendum (the DPA required when handling customer personal data under GDPR or CCPA), the Business Associate Agreement (HIPAA), and marketplace Reseller Agreements.

## Why these matter (and the anti-pattern)

Using a well-drafted, market-standard template as a starting point is far safer than the two classic mistakes: writing a contract from scratch without legal review, or copying a random contract found online (using someone else's template blindly), which often contains terms mismatched to the business, missing limitation-of-liability and indemnity clauses, or governing-law and IP provisions that quietly favor the other side. A standard template still needs to be tailored to the specific deal and reviewed by counsel, but it starts from a balanced, tested baseline.
